segments.text: Personality refers to relatively enduring patterns in how people think, feel and behave. The syllabus asks not only “what personality is” but also how it develops, how different theories explain it, and how psychologists assess it.
The simplest way to study personality is to compare perspectives. Each theory focuses on a different source of consistency and individual difference.

items.text: Determinants and development
: Personality develops through interaction among biological dispositions, learning, family and social experience, culture, life events and personal choices. Avoid a one-cause explanation.
Psychodynamic perspective

: Psychodynamic theories emphasize unconscious processes, internal conflict and early experience. They are historically important but should be discussed with awareness that not all propositions have equal empirical support.
Trait perspective
: Trait approaches describe relatively stable dimensions on which people differ. Modern trait research often organizes personality using broad trait dimensions rather than fixed “types.”
Behavioural and social-cognitive perspective
: These approaches emphasize learning, reinforcement, observation, expectations, self-efficacy and reciprocal influence among person, behaviour and environment.
Humanistic perspective
: Humanistic theories stress subjective experience, personal growth, choice and self-concept. They shifted attention toward healthy development and meaning.
Assessment techniques

: Common approaches include structured or unstructured interviews, self-report inventories, behavioural assessment and performance-based/projective techniques. Each differs in reliability, validity and purpose.
Cross-cultural issues
: A personality measure developed in one population may not work identically in another. Language, norms and cultural meanings can affect responses and interpretation.

blocks.text: What personality theories try to explain

segments.text: Personality theories address three connected questions: why people show relatively stable patterns, why individuals differ from one another and why the same person may behave differently across situations. Stability is therefore probabilistic rather than absolute. Traits predict tendencies, not identical behaviour in every context.

items.text: Temperament and biology

: Early-emerging differences in emotional reactivity and self-regulation provide part of the foundation for later personality. Genetic influence is important but operates through development and environment rather than fixing a complete adult personality at birth.
Learning and social context
: Reinforcement histories, modelling, roles, opportunities and culture shape how dispositions are expressed. A person may show confidence in familiar settings but caution in unfamiliar environments.
Central claim

: Classical psychodynamic theory emphasizes unconscious motives, conflict and the long influence of early relationships. Freud's id, ego and superego are theoretical constructs, not anatomical brain structures.
Defence mechanisms

: Defence mechanisms describe ways people may reduce psychological conflict or anxiety, such as denial or rationalization. Some concepts influenced later clinical thinking, but their measurement can be difficult.
Evaluation

: The historical influence of psychoanalysis is substantial, especially in psychotherapy and theories of unconscious processes. However, many classical developmental claims are difficult to falsify, and modern evidence does not support treating the full Freudian system as established fact.
Traits
: Traits describe relatively enduring dimensions of thought, feeling and behaviour. They summarize patterns rather than explaining every causal mechanism behind them.
Big Five

: A widely used lexical/factor-analytic model organizes personality around openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism/negative emotionality. The model has broad cross-cultural support but does not exhaust every culturally meaningful personality concept.
Person-situation interaction

: Walter Mischel's critique of broad trait prediction encouraged attention to context. Modern trait psychology generally accepts that behaviour reflects both stable tendencies and situational demands.
Reciprocal determinism
: Bandura described behaviour, personal factors and environment as mutually influencing one another. This avoids a one-way model in which either the person or environment alone causes behaviour.
Self-efficacy
: Self-efficacy is belief in one's capability to perform actions needed for a specific task. It affects effort, persistence and choice but should not be confused with general self-esteem.
Humanistic view

: Rogers emphasized self-concept, congruence and conditions supporting growth. Humanistic approaches contributed a person-centred perspective but are less precise when broad concepts are difficult to operationalize.
Self-report inventories
: Structured inventories can provide reliable standardized trait information when well designed. They remain vulnerable to careless responding, impression management and limits of self-knowledge.
Interviews and behavioural assessment
: Interviews offer context and behavioural methods examine actions in relevant situations. Reliability depends on structure, training and clear criteria.
Projective techniques

: Projective methods use ambiguous stimuli and assume responses reveal underlying processes. Some have clinical traditions, but many scoring systems have weaker reliability or validity than well-validated structured measures.
Culture

: Trait structure may show broad regularities across cultures, yet norms, response styles and meanings differ. Cross-cultural interpretation requires validated translations and appropriate comparison groups.
Prepare one comparison table covering psychodynamic, trait, behavioural/social-cognitive and humanistic approaches.
For each theory learn assumptions, main concepts, view of development, assessment link and one criticism.
Use a simple example such as shyness or persistence to show how different theories explain the same pattern.
Always add cross-cultural caution to assessment questions.

rows: Avoid this error Do not casually diagnose or label real people with personality disorders when the question is about normal personality theory.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define personality, explain determinants, compare major theoretical perspectives, describe assessment methods, then discuss cross-cultural limits.
• Personality involves enduring patterns but does not mean behaviour never changes.
• Traits describe patterns; they do not explain every action in every situation.
• Learning and social context can shape personality expression.
• Assessment methods must be interpreted with technical and cultural care.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
